lesson.menu_title: The Blank and the Headline — The First Four Seconds
lesson.menu_desc: What to say when nothing comes, and how to put the conclusion first when it does -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- The Blank and the Headline
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 4 -- The Blank and the Headline

listenings.text: I coach finance people for a living and I hear the same thing every week. Somebody asks a simple question and the answer starts in nineteen ninety eight. The reasoning is understandable. You want to give context so the conclusion makes sense, and in a written report that is exactly right. In a room it is fatal, because the listener does not know where you are going, so they cannot tell which parts matter, so they stop tracking and start waiting. And once somebody is waiting, you have lost them, and nothing you say for the next ninety seconds will land. So here is the rule I give everybody and nobody likes at first. Say the conclusion in one sentence, then say how many reasons there are, then give them. Headline, signpost, detail. If you are wrong about the conclusion, they will interrupt you in fifteen seconds instead of two minutes, and honestly that is a gift.

It happened to me in front of a board, in my second year, and I still think about it. The chairman asked me something perfectly ordinary about working capital and I lost the thread completely. Not a word. And what I did, which I would not recommend, was to keep talking, faster, hoping to arrive somewhere, and after about forty seconds one of the non executives said, quite kindly, take a moment. That was the worst part, being given the moment rather than taking it. Now I take it myself. I say, let me give you the number first, and I say the number, because a number is easier to retrieve than an argument, and by the time the number is out of my mouth the argument is back. Not once since then have I gone blank for longer than four seconds. And I have been in far harder rooms than that one.

extra_audio.text: Claire asks Fernando why the panel remembered nothing from his last answer. Fernando says he started with the context and reached the conclusion at the end. Claire explains the three parts: headline, signpost, detail. Fernando rebuilds the same answer with the conclusion in the first sentence. Claire says that version would have taken forty seconds instead of three minutes.

Nadia asks a question about working capital and Fernando draws a blank. Fernando says out loud that there are two parts to the question. Fernando names where he is going before he has arrived there. Fernando starts with a concrete number instead of the argument. Nadia says she did not notice anything and asks her follow-up.
